questions.stem: Which factor of production is the effort of software engineers writing code?

options.text: Physical capital
options.why: Not physical capital: labor fits this resource.

options.text: Entrepreneurship
options.why: Not entrepreneurship: labor fits this resource.

options.text: Land (natural resources)
options.why: Not land (natural resources): labor fits this resource.

options.text: Labor
options.why: Correct. This matches the definition of the factor.

questions.explanation: Land is natural resources, labor is human effort, physical capital is produced tools and equipment, and entrepreneurship organizes the others and bears risk.

questions.stem: A central planning agency sets production targets for every factory. Which economic system does this describe?

options.text: Command economy
options.why: Correct. This matches who makes the key allocation decisions.

options.text: Barter economy
options.why: Barter describes exchange without money, not a system of allocation.

options.text: Mixed economy
options.why: Decide who answers what, how and for whom: markets, planners, or a mix.

options.text: Market economy
options.why: Decide who answers what, how and for whom: markets, planners, or a mix.

questions.explanation: Market economies rely on prices and private decisions; command economies on central planning; mixed economies combine markets with government roles.

questions.stem: The economy shifts fully employed resources from producing consumer goods to producing capital goods. Which of the following best describes the effect on the economy's production possibilities curve (PPC)?

options.text: The economy moves to a point inside its PPC.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The PPC shifts inward.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The PPC shifts outward immediately.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The economy moves along its PPC.
options.why: Correct. This matches whether resources, technology or only their use has changed.

questions.explanation: Changes in the quantity or quality of resources or in technology shift the PPC. Unemployment moves the economy inside the curve; reallocating fully employed resources moves it along the curve.

questions.stem: A firm can sell 10 units at a price of 19 each, or 11 units at a price of 15 each. What is the marginal revenue of unit 11?

options.why: This is total revenue.
Price exceeds marginal revenue because the price cut applies to all units.
Correct. 165 − 190.
This is the price cut, not the change in revenue.

questions.explanation: TR(10) = 190; TR(11) = 165. MR = -25 (negative: demand is inelastic here).

questions.stem: How many units should a rational decision-maker choose?

options.why: Stopping here leaves units whose benefit exceeds their cost.
Stopping here leaves units whose benefit exceeds their cost.
Correct. Unit 3 is the last one whose marginal benefit is at least its marginal cost.
This unit costs more than it is worth.

questions.explanation: Keep going while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost. That holds through unit 3 (MB 29, MC 22), but not for the next unit.

questions.stem: Moving from option B to option C, what is the opportunity cost of each additional unit of cloth?

options.text: $$\frac{5}{2}$$ units of wheat
options.why: This inverts the ratio: it is cloth per unit of wheat.

options.text: $$\frac{7}{5}$$ units of wheat
options.why: This divides the total wheat at the first option instead of the amount given up.

options.text: $$\frac{2}{5}$$ units of wheat
options.why: Correct. 4 units of wheat are given up for 10 more units of cloth.

options.text: $$\frac{1}{2}$$ units of wheat
options.why: This divides totals at the new option; opportunity cost uses the changes.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost per unit of cloth = (wheat given up) ÷ (cloth gained) = 4 ÷ 10 = $$\frac{2}{5}$$. The cost rises along the table, so opportunity cost is increasing.

questions.stem: What is the marginal product of worker 6?

options.why: This is the marginal product of the previous worker.
This is average product.
This is total product, not the change in it.
Correct. 45 − 45.

questions.explanation: Marginal product = change in total product = 45 − 45 = 0. Diminishing marginal returns begin after worker 2, where MP starts falling.

questions.stem: Supply of which good is likely to be the most price-elastic?

options.text: Vintage wine from a past year
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

options.text: Beachfront land
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

options.text: T-shirts made with easily available materials and labor
options.why: Correct. Availability of substitutes, necessity, budget share, time and production flexibility drive elasticity.

options.text: Original paintings by a deceased artist
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

questions.explanation: Demand is more elastic with close substitutes, for luxuries, for large budget shares and over longer time periods. Supply is more elastic when production can expand easily.

options.text: A loss of 10,000
options.why: This is economic profit.
Implicit costs are subtracted, not added.

questions.stem: Homeowners who plant gardens make their neighborhood more attractive to neighbors. Which of the following is true?

options.text: The market produces too much; a per-unit tax could correct it.
options.why: Decide whether third parties bear a cost (negative) or receive a benefit (positive).

options.text: The market produces too little; a per-unit subsidy could correct it.
options.why: Correct. Negative externalities cause overproduction; positive ones cause underproduction.

options.text: The market produces the efficient quantity, so no policy is needed.
options.why: Decide whether third parties bear a cost (negative) or receive a benefit (positive).

options.text: The market produces too much; a per-unit subsidy could correct it.
options.why: Decide whether third parties bear a cost (negative) or receive a benefit (positive).

questions.explanation: With a negative externality MSC > MPC and the market overproduces; a Pigouvian tax fixes it. With a positive externality MSB > MPB and the market underproduces; a subsidy fixes it.

questions.stem: How is a city's street lighting best classified?

options.text: Public good: non-rival and non-excludable
options.why: Correct. Check rivalry (does one person's use reduce availability?) and excludability (can non-payers be kept out?).

options.text: Club good: non-rival and excludable
options.why: Recheck rivalry and excludability for this good.

options.text: Common resource: rival and non-excludable
options.why: Recheck rivalry and excludability for this good.

options.text: Private good: rival and excludable
options.why: Recheck rivalry and excludability for this good.

questions.explanation: Goods are classified by rivalry and excludability: private (both), public (neither), common resources (rival only), club goods (excludable only).

questions.stem: A firm lowers its price and finds that its total revenue decreases. Over this range, demand for its product is

options.text: price inelastic
options.why: Correct. Price and total revenue moved in the same direction.

options.text: perfectly elastic
options.why: With perfectly elastic demand, any price increase would lose all sales.

options.text: unit elastic
options.why: With unit elastic demand, total revenue would not change.

options.text: price elastic
options.why: Use the total revenue test: same direction means inelastic, opposite means elastic.

questions.explanation: Price fell and total revenue fell. Same-direction movements mean quantity changed by a smaller percentage than price: inelastic.

questions.stem: Demand is $$Q_d = 116 - 3P$$ and supply is $$Q_s = 12 + 5P$$. The government sets a price floor of 15. What results?

options.text: A surplus of 6 units
options.why: Compare quantity demanded with quantity supplied at the controlled price, not with the old equilibrium.

options.text: A surplus of 16 units
options.why: Correct. At 15, $$Q_d = 71$$ and $$Q_s = 87$$.

options.text: A shortage of 16 units
options.why: A binding floor (above equilibrium) creates a surplus.

options.text: No effect, because the control is not binding
options.why: Equilibrium price is 13, so a floor of 15 is binding.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is P = 13, Q = 77. At the floor of 15, quantity demanded is 71 and quantity supplied is 87: a surplus of 16.

questions.stem: Which market structure is described? A single firm with high barriers to entry can earn economic profit in the long run.

options.text: Oligopoly
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Perfect competition
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Monopolistic competition
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Monopoly
options.why: Correct. This matches the structure's long-run conditions.

questions.explanation: Perfect competition: P = MC = min ATC. Monopolistic competition: P = ATC > MC, excess capacity. Oligopoly: few interdependent firms. Monopoly: one firm, barriers, possible long-run profit.

questions.stem: A household earning 20,000 pays 2,000 in tax, and a household earning 120,000 pays 24,000. The tax is

options.text: lump-sum
options.why: A lump-sum tax is the same amount for everyone.

options.text: proportional
options.why: Compare the tax as a percentage of income, not the amount paid.

options.text: regressive
options.why: Compare the tax as a percentage of income, not the amount paid.

options.text: progressive
options.why: Correct. The rates are 10% and 20%.

questions.explanation: Tax as a share of income: 10% for the lower income and 20% for the higher. Rising share: progressive; falling: regressive; equal: proportional.

questions.stem: What is the average fixed cost of producing 4 units?

options.why: Correct. FC ÷ Q = 200 ÷ 4.
This is the marginal cost.
This is the average variable cost.
This is the average total cost.

questions.explanation: Fixed cost is the cost at zero output, 200. At 4 units: MC = 21, ATC = 65.75, AVC = 15.75, AFC = 50.

questions.stem: Every household's income doubles. Which of the following is true?

options.text: The Lorenz curve moves toward the line of equality and the Gini coefficient falls.
options.why: Think about how the shares of income held by each group change.

options.text: The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient do not change.
options.why: Correct. The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient measure relative shares, not income levels.

options.text: The Gini coefficient becomes negative.
options.why: The Gini coefficient lies between 0 and 1.

options.text: Income inequality increases and the Gini coefficient rises.
options.why: Think about how the shares of income held by each group change.

questions.explanation: The farther the Lorenz curve from the 45-degree line, the higher the Gini coefficient and the greater the inequality. Equal proportional changes in all incomes leave shares unchanged.

questions.stem: In a competitive labor market, demand for the product the workers make falls. Which of the following is most likely?

options.text: Labor supply increases; the wage falls and employment rises.
options.why: Check which curve the event shifts and read the new wage and employment.

options.text: Labor supply increases; the wage and employment fall.
options.why: Check which curve the event shifts and read the new wage and employment.

options.text: Labor demand decreases; the wage and employment fall.
options.why: Correct. Identify whether firms' MRP (demand) or workers' availability (supply) changed.

options.text: Labor supply decreases; the wage rises and employment falls.
options.why: Check which curve the event shifts and read the new wage and employment.

questions.explanation: Labor demand depends on MRP (product price and productivity). Labor supply depends on the number of available workers and entry requirements.

questions.stem: A town's only large employer, compared with what a competitive labor market would produce, hires

options.text: fewer workers at a higher wage
options.why: Restricting hiring lets the monopsonist pay a lower wage, read from the supply curve.

options.text: the same number of workers at the same wage
options.why: Monopsony power changes both employment and the wage.

options.text: fewer workers at a lower wage
options.why: Correct. It hires where MRP = MFC, with MFC above the supply curve, then pays the wage on the supply curve.

options.text: more workers at a lower wage
options.why: Because MFC exceeds the wage, the monopsonist restricts hiring.

questions.explanation: A monopsonist's MFC lies above labor supply, so MRP = MFC at a lower employment level, and the wage needed to attract those workers is also lower.

questions.stem: When consumer income rises by 50%, the quantity demanded of a good falls by 5%. The good is

options.text: an inferior good
options.why: Correct. Income elasticity = -5 ÷ 50 = -0.1.

options.text: a complement
options.why: Complements are identified with cross-price elasticity, not income elasticity.

options.text: a normal good (necessity)
options.why: Check the sign and size of the income elasticity.

options.text: a normal good (luxury)
options.why: Check the sign and size of the income elasticity.

questions.explanation: Income elasticity -0.1: negative means inferior, between 0 and 1 a necessity, above 1 a luxury.

questions.stem: Which good is likely to have the most price-elastic demand?

options.text: One particular brand of bottled water
options.why: Correct. Availability of substitutes, necessity, budget share, time and production flexibility drive elasticity.

options.text: Insulin for diabetics
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

options.text: Electricity for home heating in the short run
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

questions.explanation: Demand is more elastic with close substitutes, for luxuries, for large budget shares and over longer time periods. Supply is more elastic when production can expand easily.

questions.stem: A monopolist becomes able to perfectly price discriminate. Compared with a single-price monopoly, which is true?

options.text: Output and deadweight loss are unchanged, but price rises.
options.why: Recall the conditions for and effects of price discrimination.

options.text: Consumer surplus rises, and producer surplus falls.
options.why: Recall the conditions for and effects of price discrimination.

options.text: Output falls, and deadweight loss rises.
options.why: Recall the conditions for and effects of price discrimination.

options.text: Output rises to the efficient level, and consumer surplus falls to zero.
options.why: Correct. Price discrimination charges more to buyers with less elastic demand, requires market power and no resale, and perfect discrimination captures all surplus.

questions.explanation: Price discrimination needs market power, separable groups and no resale. The less elastic group pays more. Perfect price discrimination produces the efficient quantity with no consumer surplus.

questions.stem: Demand is $$Q_d = 32 - 2P$$ and supply is $$Q_s = 4P - 34$$. What are the equilibrium price and quantity?

options.why: Correct. Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.
At this price quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
The price and quantity are swapped.

questions.stem: Moving from option B to option C, what is the opportunity cost of each additional unit of tea?

options.text: $$\frac{2}{5}$$ units of coffee
options.why: This divides totals at the new option; opportunity cost uses the changes.

questions.stem: Producing each unit of a good imposes a constant external cost of 16 on third parties. Market demand is $$P = 96 - Q$$ and market supply (marginal private cost) is $$P = 5 + Q$$. What is the socially efficient quantity?

options.why: This is the market quantity, which ignores the external cost.
The external cost reduces the efficient quantity.
Correct. $$96 - Q = 21 + Q$$.
Set MSB = MSC: demand equals supply plus the external cost.

questions.explanation: MSC = 5 + Q + 16. Efficient quantity where MSB = MSC: 96 − Q = 21 + Q, so Q = 37.5, below the market quantity 45.5.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Firm A?

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy is to advertise.
options.why: Compare Firm A's own payoffs (the first number) for each of Firm B's choices.

options.text: Firm A has no dominant strategy.
options.why: Correct. If B advertises, A gets 6 (advertise) or 9 (not); if B does not, A gets 9 or 4.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy is not to advertise.
options.why: Compare Firm A's own payoffs (the first number) for each of Firm B's choices.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy depends on Firm B's dominant strategy.
options.why: A dominant strategy, by definition, is best whatever the other firm does.

questions.explanation: A strategy is dominant if it gives the higher payoff whichever strategy the other firm picks. Compare only Firm A's payoffs within each column.

questions.stem: At the world price of 8, domestic consumers buy 131 units and domestic producers supply 49. A tariff of 2 raises the domestic price to 10, where consumers buy 121 and producers supply 60. How much revenue does the tariff raise?

options.why: Correct. 2 × imports of 61.
The tariff applies only to imports, not to domestic production.
Use imports after the tariff.
Revenue is the tariff per unit, not the full price.

questions.explanation: Imports after the tariff = 121 − 60 = 61. Tariff revenue = 2 × 61 = 122.

This worker's MRP is below the wage.

questions.explanation: MRP = MP × P: 168, 133, 112, 77, 42, 7. Hire while MRP ≥ wage (58): 4 workers.

questions.stem: In the market for gasoline, buyers expect gasoline prices to rise sharply next month. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity of gasoline?

options.text: Price will decrease; quantity will increase
options.why: Not this one: Price will increase.

options.text: Price will increase; quantity will increase

options.why: Not this one: quantity will increase.

options.why: Not this one: Price will increase, and quantity will increase.

questions.explanation: Expected higher future prices increase current demand: demand increases. A demand shift moves price and quantity in the same direction.

questions.stem: Which outcome is the Nash equilibrium?

options.text: Firm A does not advertise, Firm B does not advertise
options.why: At least one firm would switch strategies from this cell to increase its own payoff.

options.text: Firm A advertises, Firm B advertises
options.why: At least one firm would switch strategies from this cell to increase its own payoff.

options.why: Correct. Neither firm can raise its own payoff by changing only its own strategy.

options.text: Firm A does not advertise, Firm B advertises
options.why: At least one firm would switch strategies from this cell to increase its own payoff.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm's minimum average variable cost is 28 and its minimum average total cost is 35. The market price is 26. What should the firm do?

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Correct. Price is below minimum AVC.

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms enter the industry.
options.why: Firms do not enter an industry that is making losses.

options.text: Produce in the short run at a loss; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Produce in the short run; it earns an economic profit, so firms enter in the long run.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

questions.explanation: Short run: produce if P ≥ min AVC (28). Long run: entry if P > min ATC (35), exit if P < min ATC. Here P = 26.

questions.stem: The wage paid to every worker rises. How are the firm's short-run cost curves affected?

options.text: Only MC shifts up.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: MC, AVC and ATC all shift down.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: ATC shifts down; MC shifts up.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: MC, AVC and ATC all shift up.
options.why: Correct. Fixed costs affect only average fixed and total costs; variable costs affect marginal and average variable costs too.

questions.explanation: A change in fixed cost shifts AFC and ATC but leaves MC and AVC unchanged. A change in a per-unit (variable) cost shifts MC, AVC and ATC.

questions.stem: In a market with straight-line supply and demand, the equilibrium price is 24 and the equilibrium quantity is 12. The demand curve meets the price axis at 30, and the supply curve meets it at 7. What is consumer surplus?

options.why: Surplus is a triangle: multiply by one half.
This is total surplus.
This is producer surplus.

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 12 × (30 − 24) = 36.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive, constant-cost industry is in long-run equilibrium. Market demand then increases permanently. Which of the following describes the long-run adjustment?

options.text: Each firm's demand curve becomes downward sloping.
options.why: Firms in perfect competition remain price takers.

options.text: Firms exit, market supply decreases, and the price rises further.
options.why: The direction of entry or exit is reversed.

options.text: Firms enter, market supply increases, and the price falls back to minimum ATC.
options.why: Correct. Short-run profits attract entry.

options.text: The price stays permanently higher, and firms keep earning economic profit.
options.why: Free entry and exit eliminate economic profit and losses in the long run.

questions.explanation: The higher price creates economic profits. Firms enter, shifting market supply right until price returns to minimum ATC and economic profit is zero.

questions.stem: Demand is $$Q_d = 78 - 2P$$ and supply is $$Q_s = 26 + 2P$$. The government sets a price ceiling of 10. What results?

options.text: A shortage of 6 units
options.why: Compare quantity demanded with quantity supplied at the controlled price, not with the old equilibrium.

options.text: No effect, because the control is not binding
options.why: Equilibrium price is 13, so a ceiling of 10 is binding.

options.text: A surplus of 12 units
options.why: A binding ceiling (below equilibrium) creates a shortage.

options.text: A shortage of 12 units
options.why: Correct. At 10, $$Q_d = 58$$ and $$Q_s = 46$$.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is P = 13, Q = 52. At the ceiling of 10, quantity demanded is 58 and quantity supplied is 46: a shortage of 12.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive, constant-cost industry is in long-run equilibrium. Market demand then decreases permanently. Which of the following describes the long-run adjustment?

options.text: The price stays permanently lower, and firms keep making losses.
options.why: Free entry and exit eliminate economic profit and losses in the long run.

options.text: Firms exit, market supply decreases, and the price rises back to minimum ATC.
options.why: Correct. Short-run losses cause exit.

options.text: Each firm's demand curve becomes downward sloping.
options.why: Firms in perfect competition remain price takers.

options.text: Firms enter, market supply increases, and the price falls further.
options.why: The direction of entry or exit is reversed.

questions.explanation: The lower price creates economic losses. Firms exit, shifting market supply left until price returns to minimum ATC and economic profit is zero.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.text: Neither country can gain from trade.
options.why: Different opportunity costs always allow mutually beneficial trade.

options.text: Country Y has a comparative advantage in bicycles, and Country X in chairs.
options.why: Correct. One unit of bicycles costs 1.00 chairs in X and 0.40 chairs in Y.

options.why: This reverses the comparison of opportunity costs.

options.text: Country X has a comparative advantage in both goods.
options.why: No country can have a comparative advantage in both goods; opportunity costs are reciprocals.

questions.explanation: Compare opportunity costs, not output levels. In X, one bicycles costs $$1$$ chairs; in Y, $$\frac{2}{5}$$ chairs. The country with the lower cost has the comparative advantage in bicycles; the other has it in chairs.

questions.stem: A regulator sets the price a natural monopoly may charge at the level where the demand curve intersects average total cost. Which of the following results?

options.text: The firm earns larger profits than without regulation.
options.why: Regulation lowers the price the firm can charge.

options.text: The allocatively efficient quantity is produced.
options.why: Efficiency needs P = MC; at P = ATC output is still below the efficient level.

options.text: Output falls below the unregulated monopoly level.
options.why: A price ceiling below the monopoly price raises output.

options.text: The firm earns zero economic profit (a fair return).
options.why: Correct. At P = ATC, total revenue equals total cost.

questions.explanation: The socially optimal price (P = MC) gives the efficient quantity but, for a natural monopoly, a loss. The fair-return price (P = ATC) gives zero economic profit with output between the monopoly and efficient levels.

questions.stem: A monopsonist can hire 5 workers at a wage of 14 each, or 6 workers at a wage of 17 each. What is the marginal factor cost of worker 6?

options.why: Correct. 102 − 70.
This is total labor cost.
This is only the raise for one worker.
MFC exceeds the wage because the higher wage is paid to all workers.

questions.explanation: Total cost rises from 70 to 102, so MFC = 32, greater than the wage of 17.

questions.stem: A monopsonist can hire 9 workers at a wage of 11 each, or 10 workers at a wage of 12 each. What is the marginal factor cost of worker 10?

options.why: This is only the raise for one worker.
This is total labor cost.
Correct. 120 − 99.
MFC exceeds the wage because the higher wage is paid to all workers.

questions.explanation: Total cost rises from 99 to 120, so MFC = 21, greater than the wage of 12.

questions.stem: A firm earns total revenue of 280,000 and pays explicit costs of 260,000. The owner could earn 70,000 working elsewhere. What is the firm's accounting profit?

options.why: Implicit costs are subtracted, not added.

options.text: A loss of 50,000
options.why: This is economic profit.
Correct. Revenue minus explicit costs.
This subtracts only the implicit cost.

questions.stem: In a competitive market, demand decreases and, at the same time, supply increases. Which of the following describes the change in equilibrium?

options.text: Price will decrease; quantity cannot be determined
options.why: Correct. Shift each curve separately: one variable moves the same way in both cases, the other depends on the sizes of the shifts.

options.text: Price will increase; quantity cannot be determined
options.why: Not this one: Price will decrease.

options.text: Price cannot be determined; quantity will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price will decrease, and quantity is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Price will increase; quantity will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price will decrease, and quantity is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: The demand shift alone moves price down and quantity down. The supply shift alone moves price down and quantity up. Where the effects agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

questions.stem: Which condition is necessary for a firm to price discriminate?

options.text: The firm sells an identical product in a perfectly competitive market.
options.why: Recall the conditions for and effects of price discrimination.

options.text: The firm can prevent buyers from reselling the good.
options.why: Correct. Price discrimination charges more to buyers with less elastic demand, requires market power and no resale, and perfect discrimination captures all surplus.

options.text: The firm's marginal cost is zero.
options.why: Recall the conditions for and effects of price discrimination.

options.text: All buyers have the same willingness to pay.
options.why: Recall the conditions for and effects of price discrimination.

questions.explanation: Price discrimination needs market power, separable groups and no resale. The less elastic group pays more. Perfect price discrimination produces the efficient quantity with no consumer surplus.

questions.stem: When the price of a good rises from 4 to 10, the quantity demanded falls from 260 to 210. Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity of demand, and is demand elastic or inelastic?

options.text: 4.03, elastic
options.why: This divides the percentage change in price by the percentage change in quantity: upside down.

options.text: 0.25, inelastic
options.why: Correct. Percentage changes use the averages of the two values.

options.text: 0.25, elastic
options.why: The value is right but the classification is wrong: elastic means greater than 1.

options.text: 0.13, inelastic
options.why: This uses the starting values instead of the midpoint method.

questions.explanation: %ΔQ = 50 ÷ 235 ≈ 21.3%; %ΔP = 6 ÷ 7 ≈ 85.7%. Elasticity ≈ 0.25, so demand is inelastic.

questions.stem: A consumer spends her whole budget on goods A and B. For the last units bought, the marginal utility of A is 27 with a price of 3, and the marginal utility of B is 20 with a price of 5. To maximize utility, she should

options.text: buy more of good B and less of the other good
options.why: Compare marginal utility per dollar, not marginal utility alone.

options.text: buy more of good A and less of the other good
options.why: Correct. Good A gives 9 utils per dollar; good B gives 4.

options.text: buy more of the good with the higher marginal utility, A
options.why: A higher marginal utility does not mean a better buy if the price is also higher.

options.text: keep her purchases unchanged
options.why: The marginal utilities per dollar are not equal, so a better bundle exists.

questions.explanation: MU per dollar: A = 27 ÷ 3 = 9; B = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Shift spending toward A until the ratios are equal.

questions.stem: Before a per-unit tax of 4, the market price is 12. After the tax, buyers pay 13 and sellers keep 9. Which of the following is true?

options.text: Sellers bear more of the tax, so supply is relatively more elastic.
options.why: The side that cannot easily adjust (more inelastic) bears more of the tax.

options.text: Sellers bear more of the tax, so supply is relatively more inelastic.
options.why: Correct. Buyers pay 1 more; sellers receive 3 less.

options.text: Buyers bear more of the tax, so demand is relatively more inelastic.
options.why: Compare how much each side's price changed.

options.text: The side the law taxes pays the whole tax.
options.why: The burden depends on elasticities, not on who is legally taxed.

questions.explanation: Buyers' price rose by 1 and sellers' price fell by 3. The more inelastic side bears more of the burden.

questions.stem: A firm uses labor (wage 10) and capital (rental price 12). The marginal product of labor is 70 and the marginal product of capital is 60. To produce its output at the lowest cost, the firm should

options.text: keep its input mix unchanged
options.why: The marginal products per dollar are unequal, so costs can be lowered.

options.text: use more capital and less of the other input
options.why: Compare marginal product per dollar, not marginal product alone.

options.text: use more of both inputs
options.why: To minimize cost for a given output, shift spending between inputs rather than adding both.

options.text: use more labor and less of the other input
options.why: Correct. Labor yields 7 units per dollar; capital yields 5.

questions.explanation: MP per dollar: labor 70 ÷ 10 = 7; capital 60 ÷ 12 = 5. Shift toward labor until the ratios are equal.

questions.stem: The government imposes a lump-sum tax (a fixed amount, regardless of output) on a profit-maximizing monopolist. In the short run, what happens to the monopolist's output and price?

options.text: Output falls and price rises.
options.why: Only a change in marginal cost changes the MR = MC quantity.

options.text: Output rises and price falls.
options.why: Taxes do not lower the monopolist's costs.

options.text: The monopolist passes the full tax on to consumers with no change in output.
options.why: Output depends on where MR equals MC.

options.text: Output and price do not change; profit falls.
options.why: Correct. A lump-sum tax raises fixed cost, not marginal cost.

questions.explanation: A lump-sum tax is a fixed cost: ATC rises but MC is unchanged, so the profit-maximizing output and price stay the same and profit falls.

questions.stem: The price of raw materials used in each unit falls. How are the firm's short-run cost curves affected?

options.text: Only MC shifts up.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: MC, AVC and ATC all shift up.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: ATC and AFC shift up; MC and AVC do not change.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: MC, AVC and ATC all shift down.
options.why: Correct. Fixed costs affect only average fixed and total costs; variable costs affect marginal and average variable costs too.

questions.explanation: A change in fixed cost shifts AFC and ATC but leaves MC and AVC unchanged. A change in a per-unit (variable) cost shifts MC, AVC and ATC.

questions.stem: A regulator sets the price a natural monopoly may charge at the level where the demand curve intersects marginal cost. Which of the following results?

options.text: The firm earns zero economic profit.
options.why: With falling ATC above MC, pricing at MC causes a loss.

options.text: Output falls below the unregulated monopoly level.
options.why: A price ceiling below the monopoly price raises output.

options.text: The allocatively efficient quantity is produced, but the firm may need a subsidy because price is below average total cost.
options.why: Correct. At P = MC, output is efficient, but a natural monopoly's ATC exceeds MC.

options.text: The firm earns larger profits than without regulation.
options.why: Regulation lowers the price the firm can charge.

questions.explanation: The socially optimal price (P = MC) gives the efficient quantity but, for a natural monopoly, a loss. The fair-return price (P = ATC) gives zero economic profit with output between the monopoly and efficient levels.

questions.stem: How many units should the firm produce to maximize profit?

options.why: Producing more adds units whose marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.
Producing more adds units whose marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.
Correct. Unit 5 is the last one whose marginal cost (22) is at most the price (MR) of 25.
This unit costs more than the price it sells for.

questions.explanation: For a price taker, MR = P = 25. Produce every unit whose MC is at most 25: units 1 to 5.

questions.stem: A monopolist faces demand $$P = 17 - Q$$ and has constant marginal cost and average total cost of 5. What is the profit-maximizing quantity?

options.why: This is where demand reaches a price of zero.
MR = MC sets the quantity; MR has twice the slope of demand.
This is the efficient quantity where P = MC.
Correct. $$MR = 17 - 2Q = 5$$ gives $$Q = 6$$, so $$P = 11$$.

questions.explanation: MR = 17 − 2Q. Setting MR = MC: Q = 6; price from demand: P = 11. Profit = (11 − 5) × 6 = 36. The efficient quantity is 12, so DWL = ½ × 6 × 6 = 18.

parts.prompt: Describe correctly labeled side-by-side graphs for the market and for the typical firm. On the firm's graph show MR, MC, ATC and the profit-maximizing quantity.

rubric.criterion: Market graph with supply and demand setting the price.
rubric.example: Market price 25 at the intersection of S and D.

rubric.criterion: Firm's horizontal demand = MR = P at the market price.
Firm produces where MR = MC, with ATC drawn consistently.
rubric.example: q = 90 where MC crosses MR; ATC at 21.

parts.prompt: Calculate the firm's economic profit or loss. Show your work.
Should the firm continue to produce in the short run? Explain using cost curves.

rubric.example: Yes: price 25 is at least AVC 18, so producing covers variable costs and part of the fixed cost of 270.

parts.prompt: What happens to the number of firms in the industry in the long run? Explain.

rubric.example: Firms enter because existing firms earn economic profits.

parts.prompt: After all long-run adjustments, compare the market price with the typical firm's minimum average total cost.

rubric.example: In long-run equilibrium, P = minimum ATC, and economic profit is zero.

parts.prompt: Calculate the marginal revenue product of the third worker.
How many workers will the firm hire? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct number with the MRP ≥ wage rule.
rubric.example: 2: MRP is at least the wage of 68 for workers 1 to 2 only.

parts.prompt: If the price of the product rises, what happens to the firm's demand for labor? Explain.

rubric.example: Each worker's MRP = MP × P rises, so labor demand shifts right.

parts.prompt: Does Alpha have a dominant strategy? Explain using the payoffs.

rubric.criterion: Correct answer with the payoff comparison.
rubric.example: No. Alpha's best choice depends on Beta: against High it prefers High, against Low it prefers Low.

parts.prompt: Does Beta have a dominant strategy? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Lists the Nash equilibrium cells (or states there is none in pure strategies).
rubric.example: There is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

parts.prompt: Suppose the government pays Alpha a bonus of 4 whenever Alpha chooses Low price. Recompute Alpha's payoffs. Does Alpha now have a dominant strategy?

rubric.criterion: Adds the bonus to both Low-price payoffs and evaluates dominance.
rubric.example: Low-price payoffs become 6 and 18. Yes, Low price.
